summary: Provides the NETCONF binding for dynamic subscriptions, covering both subscribed notifications and YANG-Push. It describes how a NETCONF client creates and manages subscriptions to event streams and datastore updates over a NETCONF session.

eli5.summary: This explains how to sign up for live updates using one particular way of talking to network devices, called NETCONF.

questions: how does yang push work over netconf
what happens to a subscription when the netconf session ends
subtitle: How a NETCONF client asks a device to push it events and datastore updates, and what happens on the session.

tldr.problem: Dynamic subscriptions to event streams and datastore updates are defined generically, but a concrete transport must say how they behave on a real protocol session.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8640 binds them to NETCONF: subscription RPCs and notifications travel on the NETCONF session that established the subscription, XML encoding and the NETCONF stream are mandatory, and errors are reported as NETCONF rpc-error elements with defined mappings.
tldr.outcome: A NETCONF client can subscribe to events and YANG datastore updates, and the subscription ends if its session ends.

today: RFC 8640 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2019. The metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it is the NETCONF binding for the subscription mechanisms of RFC 8639 and RFC 8641.

sections.title: What This Document Binds
sections.content:
This document specifies how a stream of events that forms part of a dynamic subscription is bound to the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF, RFC 6241). Dynamic subscriptions themselves are defined in RFC 8639. Because RFC 8641 is built on RFC 8639, this binding also lets a NETCONF client request, and receive, updates from a YANG datastore on a NETCONF server.

The RFC assumes the reader knows the terminology of RFC 8639 (dynamic subscription, event stream, notification message, publisher, receiver, subscriber, subscription). It defines no additional terms.
sections.eli5: The general rules for signing up for updates already exist. This document just says how to follow them when you talk to a device using NETCONF.

sections.title: Coexisting With create-subscription
sections.content:
A publisher may support the dynamic subscription RPCs of RFC 8639 and the older create-subscription RPC of RFC 5277 at the same time. A single NETCONF transport session, however, MUST NOT support both a subscription from this specification and one created by create-subscription.

To enforce that, a solution MUST reply with an rpc-error whose error-tag is operation-not-supported in two cases: when create-subscription arrives on a session that already has an established RFC 8639 subscription, and when establish-subscription arrives on a session where create-subscription has already created one.

If a publisher supports this specification but not subscriptions via RFC 5277, it MUST NOT advertise urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:notification:1.0.
sections.eli5: A phone line can use the new sign-up style or the old one, but not both at once. If you try to mix them, the device says no.

sections.title: Mandatory Support
sections.content:
The encode-xml feature of RFC 8639 MUST be supported, which means XML is a valid encoding for RPCs, state change notifications and subscribed content.

A NETCONF publisher that supports event stream subscription via RFC 8639 MUST also support the NETCONF event stream identified in that document.
sections.eli5: Every device that offers this must be able to speak in XML and must offer the standard NETCONF news channel, so clients know what to expect.

sections.title: Sessions and Notification Messages
sections.content:
Dynamic subscriptions are managed with the RPCs defined in RFC 8641 and RFC 8639. If the NETCONF session used for establish-subscription terminates, the subscription MUST be terminated. Any modify-subscription, delete-subscription or resync-subscription RPC MUST be sent on the same NETCONF session on which the subscription was established.

Notification messages MUST be encoded in a notification message as defined in Section 4 of RFC 5277, with eventTime set to the event occurrence time. For dynamic subscriptions, all notification messages MUST use the session used by the establish-subscription RPC.

One session can carry several subscriptions, and notifications for each arrive on that same session.
sections.eli5: Your sign-up only lasts as long as your phone call. You have to change or cancel it on the same call, and the updates come to you on that call too.

sections.title: Error Responses
sections.content:
When a subscription RPC fails, the NETCONF reply MUST include an rpc-error element populated as follows. The error-type is application. The error-tag corresponds to the error identity, for example invalid-value for dscp-unavailable, encoding-unsupported, filter-unsupported and no-such-subscription, resource-denied for insufficient-resources, and operation-not-supported for replay-unsupported. The datastore errors from RFC 8641 have their own mappings, such as too-big for update-too-big.

The error-severity is error (this MAY be included). The error-app-tag carries the identity in the form modulename:identityname, for example ietf-subscribed-notifications:no-such-subscription.

For failed establish-subscription or modify-subscription requests, an error-info node may carry XML hints about parameter settings that might succeed next time. The yang-data in it SHOULD NOT include the optional reason leaf, as that would repeat the error-app-tag. Deletion, kill and resync errors need no error-info, because the subscription-id is their only input.
sections.eli5: When a request fails, the device sends back a standard note saying what went wrong, and sometimes a hint, such as a different time interval that would work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document adds no security considerations for dynamic subscriptions beyond those in RFC 8639, with one refinement based on NETCONF being connection-oriented. If a buggy or compromised subscriber sends many establish-subscription requests, the subscriptions accumulate and may use up system resources.

In that situation subscriptions MAY be terminated by terminating the underlying NETCONF session. The publisher MAY also suspend or terminate a subset of the active subscriptions on that session to reclaim resources and keep the others running normally.
sections.eli5: If one caller keeps signing up for hundreds of updates, the device can hang up on them, which cancels everything they signed up for.
